items.title: Famine in 1944 affected the grandchildren of survivors
items.claim: The Dutch Hongerwinter (1944-1945) caused severe famine for several months. Decades later, the GRANDchildren of women pregnant during the famine showed altered methylation patterns and different rates of metabolic disease — even though they were never themselves underfed.
items.prompt: How does an environmental stress affect three generations?

options.text: Epigenetic marks (especially DNA methylation patterns) acquired during fetal development can persist into adulthood; some can affect germline cells, allowing the next generation to inherit the modified pattern
It must be a DNA sequence mutation caused by famine
Famine alters social behaviour passed to grandchildren culturally

items.reveal_title: Heijmans, Tobi and colleagues — the Hongerwinter epigenetic study
items.reveal:
Heijmans et al. (2008) compared DNA methylation in adults who had been in utero during the Dutch famine to their unexposed siblings. The famine-exposed showed less methylation at the IGF2 gene 60 years later.

More recent work has shown some methylation marks pass to grandchildren, with associated health correlates.

This is not classical Lamarckism (inheritance of acquired characteristics through soft inheritance). Methylation marks are mostly cleared between generations, but some escape erasure. The mechanisms are still being mapped.

Distinguishing real intergenerational inheritance from confounders (in utero exposure, shared environment) requires careful study design. Animal models (rodents) have been used to confirm causal mechanisms.
items.why: Inheritance is taught as DNA sequence transmission. Some heritable information is encoded above the sequence, in modifications to DNA and chromatin — and famine can leave its mark across decades.

items.title: Information can flow from RNA back to DNA
items.claim: Crick's central dogma: DNA makes RNA makes protein. The arrow goes one way: DNA to RNA. But retroviruses — including HIV — carry an enzyme that copies their RNA genome back into DNA.
items.prompt: What does reverse transcription mean for the dogma?

options.text: The central dogma is wrong and discredited

Crick's original statement was about residue-level sequence transfer; reverse transcription does flow RNA-to-DNA, but the forbidden flow (protein-to-DNA) has never been observed — the dogma is more nuanced than the textbook version
Reverse transcription is a lab artefact

items.reveal_title: Crick's original dogma was more sophisticated than the cartoon
items.reveal:
Crick (1958) explicitly listed which residue-level transfers were possible (DNA to DNA, DNA to RNA, RNA to protein) and which were special transfers (RNA to RNA, RNA to DNA) — possible but not normally done. He also listed forbidden transfers (anything starting from protein).

Reverse transcriptase, discovered by Temin and Baltimore in 1970 (1975 Nobel), is the canonical 'special transfer'. HIV uses it to integrate into the host genome. Some retrotransposons in our own genomes do it constantly.

The forbidden transfers (protein to DNA, protein to RNA, protein to protein) remain forbidden. The dogma, taken literally as Crick wrote it, still stands.
items.why: Pop science presents 'the central dogma' as a rigid one-way arrow. The real dogma is a constraint on which directions sequence information can flow in, and reverse transcription was always allowed.

items.title: A 32,000-year-old seed grew into a flower
items.claim: In 2012, Russian scientists germinated seeds from a Silene stenophylla plant buried in Siberian permafrost about 32,000 years ago. Even outside such extremes, soil under most fields holds millions of viable seeds per hectare — a 'seed bank' waiting for the right conditions.
items.prompt: How can seeds survive so long?

options.text: Dehydrated seeds enter a state of suspended metabolism (similar to tardigrades): low water content, vitrified protective sugars (raffinose, sucrose), late-embryogenesis-abundant (LEA) proteins, and physical/chemical dormancy mechanisms that block germination until cues like fire, scarification or freeze-thaw are met

items.reveal:
Seeds drop into soil constantly. Most germinate or die within a year. Some develop dormancy — physical (hard coat blocks water entry until scratched), physiological (chemical inhibitors must be degraded), or morphological (embryo must mature further).

A typical arable field has ~20-50 million weed seeds per hectare in the top 25 cm of soil. Many remain viable for 10-100 years. A few species (Verbascum, Chenopodium) have been germinated from soil samples 60+ years old.

The Silene seeds were buried by ice age squirrels in their burrows. Russian scientists grew tissue from the placenta of the immature fruits and regenerated the plants — not strictly seeds, but the same physiology.

Oldest unequivocally germinated seed: 2000-year-old date palm from Masada (Israel), germinated 2005.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault (2008) stores ~1 million seed accessions at -18 C to preserve global crop diversity. The principle is the same as natural seed banks: dehydration plus cold preserves embryos near-indefinitely.

Disturbing a forest soil triggers mass germination as buried weed seeds suddenly see light. The 'memory' of the soil shapes what grows after disturbance.
items.why: Seeds look inert. Inside is a paused embryo, sometimes thousands of years on hold, waiting for the chemistry of damp soil and warmth to resume the life it interrupted.
